facts.d: the advantage exists only for ultra-narrow, actively managed positions, a class already falsified in late August
facts.e: verdict 08.09: no; Uniswap stays the venue for the wide position on this pair

reference: Checked on 08.09: on Aerodrome a position staked in the gauge earns only AERO emissions (the fees go to voters), and the displayed emission APR is computed on liquidity staked in the active tick ±1 tick, a band of about 0.3%. A ±40% position holds about 0.5% of that liquidity, so it would earn roughly 4 to 6% a year in AERO, a token with about 10.9% yearly inflation, against roughly 5 to 11% a year in fees on Uniswap with no token to sell. The LP crowd on Aerodrome sits about 10x tighter, so a wide position gets crumbs; the advantage exists only for ultra-narrow, actively managed positions, the class the project had falsified in late August. question: What does an UNMAPPED verdict mean in the candidate funnel?

facts.a: the verdict when a ranked pool cannot be mapped to its on-chain address (token outside the dictionary of majors, or the token0/token1 sanity check disagrees); manual review, the funnel never guesses addresses

reference: The funnel validates pools from the DefiLlama ranking, and first maps each one to its on-chain address through a dictionary of known major tokens per network, factory.getPool and a sanity check of token0/token1. When a token is outside the dictionary or the sanity check disagrees, the verdict is UNMAPPED: the pool goes to manual review and the funnel never guesses an address or runs on silently wrong data. Exotic pairs without an ETH/BTC or stable leg are UNMAPPED by rule. Eligibility and OPEN proposals skip FAIL and UNMAPPED pools. In the first full backfill (25.08) all 5 candidates were mapped, zero UNMAPPED.

question: How was the option of confirming transactions done technically, that is, what happened after clicking to confirm the creation of a new LP position?

facts.a: cockpit path: the OPEN card's [Open] reads the pool on demand (slot0, liquidity) and opens the position window for a new position
facts.b: the window builds the mint with the same functions as the manual form (createPosition, prepareAddLiquidityTransaction)

reference: The corpus records two paths. The one used for real positions is the cockpit: an OPEN proposal card has an [Open] button that reads the pool on demand (slot0 and liquidity over RPC) and opens the position window for a new position (no NFT yet). That window reads the wallet's balances and allowances, asks for token approvals where needed and builds the mint with the same functions as the manual add-liquidity form (createPosition and prepareAddLiquidityTransaction, rewritten on the Uniswap SDK on 10.08); before signing, each action switches the wallet to the right network and takes a fresh wallet client, and the owner signs in the wallet (Rabby). After signing (fixes of 27.08, from the first real entry) the window waits for the receipt, re-reads balances and allowances, and after a successful mint closes with a toast confirming the new position.

question: What is the wide-score used in the RANKING WIDE section?

facts.a: score = c_class * apy_min - 0.6 * (sigma^2/8) * g(w): fees of a wide position minus a volatility drag
facts.b: fee = the minimum of the APY windows (penalty for episodic fees)
facts.c: implemented 01.09 as scripts/wide-score.ts (funnel v2, floor 1)

reference: A score for ranking the whole pool universe for the product's wide position: score = c_class * apy_min - 0.6 * (sigma^2/8) * g(w), the fee income of a wide position minus a volatility drag, with the fee taken as the minimum of the APY windows (a penalty for episodic fees). It was implemented on 01.09 as scripts/wide-score.ts (funnel v2, floor 1) and from 02.09 ran as a pipeline step that writes .bot/wide-ranking.json, shown in the morning report as RANKING WIDE (top 10) next to the old ranking, for observation.

question: How was a position rebalanced, that is, how were the ranges moved: was it the same position or did a new one have to be opened, and did it happen automatically or did a new transaction have to be made?

facts.a: not automatic: approving a rebalance proposal meant two or three signatures in Rabby, in order
facts.b: step 1: one multicall on the NFT position manager, decreaseLiquidity 100% + collect
facts.c: step 2: a swap evening out the token proportions in the same pool, skipped when the deviation is under 2% of value
facts.d: step 3: mint of the new range, rebuilt from the actual balances just before sending (extra approve if needed)
facts.e: progress saved in localStorage: a failure mid-way leaves the funds in the wallet and the UI offers 'finish step 2/3'

reference: A range cannot be moved on an existing Uniswap v3 position, so a rebalance closed the old position and opened a new one, and nothing happened automatically: approving a rebalance proposal meant two or three signatures in Rabby, in order. Step 1 is one multicall on the NFT position manager, decreaseLiquidity of 100% plus collect, so fees come out with the liquidity; step 2 is a swap that evens out the token proportions for the new range (exactInputSingle on SwapRouter02 in the same pool), skipped when the deviation is under 2% of the value; step 3 is the mint of the new range, rebuilt just before sending from the actual balances (the plan only holds an estimate), with an extra approval if the real amount exceeds the approved one. Progress is saved in the browser (localStorage), so a failure in the middle leaves the funds safe in the wallet and the window offers to finish the remaining step (for example 'finish step 2/3').
notes: Owner's questions 3 and 4 merged into one item in his words (Polish originals: "czy rebalancing robil sie automatycznie czy trzeba bylo zawierac nowa transakcje?" and "w jaki sposob robil sie rebalancing pozycji, przestawienie zakresow? czy byly to te same pozycje czy trzeba bylo otwierac nowe?"). question: Why did HOMOS stick to major tokens instead of the exotic pools that advertised much higher yields?

facts.a: 10.08 meta-backtest: exotics 74.8% vs majors 50.7% fee-APR, but without impermanent loss
facts.b: tick-level WTAO/WETH 1% (90 days, 10 750 swaps): real passive fee yield ~5-20%/yr, result dominated by the token's beta; narrow ranges realise losses
facts.c: 10.08: exotic sleeve 0%, majors-only confirmed by a third independent test; an exotic is a bet on the token, not an LP strategy
facts.d: 11.08 correction: the table was in WTAO units (a fall, not a rise); token beta -70%/yr crushes LP alpha ~+7 pp; majors-only stays

reference: Because the advertised yields did not survive a test with real swaps. The pool-selection meta-backtest of 10.08 showed exotic pools at 74.8% fee-APR against 50.7% for majors, but without impermanent loss. A tick-level backtest of WTAO/WETH 1% on mainnet (90 days, 10 750 swaps) then showed a real fee yield of about 5-20% a year for a passive position, the pool's result dominated by the token's own price, and narrow ranges on a trending exotic realising losses (±5%: $1 316 of fees but -33.8 points vs HODL). On 10.08 the exotic sleeve was set to 0% and the majors-only filter counted as confirmed by a third independent test; exposure to an exotic was a bet on the token, not an LP strategy. On 11.08 that table turned out to be in the wrong units (WTAO treated as a $1 stable, so the 'uptrend' was a fall, HODL -70.5% a year); the reasoning was corrected (the token's beta of -70% a year crushes an LP alpha of about +7 points) and majors-only stayed.
notes: Medium. A trap: the 10.08 table says the regime was rising (+74.9%); the 11.08 correction reverses it. Held-out batch 5 (2026-11-26), written by CC-Mac; review file ai/eval/review/heldout-batch-5.md.

question: How were the rebalance swaps protected against MEV sandwich attacks?
reference: The corpus has the requirement but no implementation. question: Which machine-learning model did the bot use to predict where the price would go?
reference: None was used or built. The only mention of machine learning in the corpus is a literature finding from the 26.08 review: ML and reinforcement learning give results on the scale of the project's own experiments, not a breakthrough. The project's question was whether a rules-based strategy with no discretion and no forecasting could beat holding the same two tokens, and the bot's choices came from fixed rules calibrated in backtests (pool ranking by 7-day fee yield, range width w = k x sigma x sqrt(7d) from measured volatility).
